- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.

Sample text:
---
The shortest item in the lost-property ledger was a tooth.

I found the entry in my second week at the municipal swimming pool, while looking for a man’s missing glasses. The ledger went back to 1983. In those days the staff had written in green fountain pen. *One tooth, bottom of deep end*, someone had recorded, then, in the column headed CLAIMED BY: *Boy who lost it.*

I liked the confidence of that. No demand for a description.

By the time I worked there, we had a clear plastic bin for goggles, a wire basket for towels, and a little safe for anything worth more than twenty pounds. Wedding rings lived in the safe beside a single hearing aid and an envelope containing forty Canadian dollars. The glasses were on the man’s head. He discovered them himself and asked me, quite seriously, not to put the incident in the book.

Most people knew exactly what they’d lost. One woman could describe her daughter’s swimsuit down to a loose thread under the left arm, though the daughter, standing beside her in a towel, maintained that she had never seen the swimsuit before. But every Thursday an older man in a shirt buttoned to the throat would ask whether anything had turned up.

“What sort of thing?” I asked the first time.

“Oh, I’ll know it.”

I let him look through the goggles. He took his time.

His name was Leonard. He didn’t swim. His wife had swum there for thirty years, he told me, and had once come home wearing somebody else’s shoes. Same make, same colour, half a size larger. She’d been delighted. “At last,” she’d said, “these bloody things are breaking in.”

I assumed his wife had died. This was because I was twenty and assumed anyone mentioned in the past tense was dead. In fact she’d taken up bowling.

“She likes a sport where she can keep her glasses on,” he said.

“Is she missing something?”

“Almost certainly.”

By October I had worked out that Leonard came on Thursdays because the number six bus changed drivers outside the pool. His daughter drove the morning route. She had seven minutes between getting off the bus and getting into the van that took her back to the depot. Sometimes he brought her a sandwich. Sometimes they stood smoking together under the NO SMOKING sign, carefully dropping their ash into his empty sandwich box. Looking through lost property was what he did if he arrived early.

One Thursday he found what he was looking for.

It was a small blue mitten, stiff with dried pool water, with a white rabbit knitted into the back. He turned it over. A name tape had been sewn inside the cuff.

“Good Lord,” he said. “I sewed that in.”

The name was Ruth Bell. His daughter’s name. She’d worn the mittens as a child, he said, and hadn’t they been a nuisance, because the rabbits meant there was a right and a wrong one, unlike a sensible pair of mittens?

I was already constructing the story. The mitten had spent thirty years behind a radiator. A workman had dislodged it. It had come back to the man who sewed the tape into its cuff. I could see the photograph in the local paper: Leonard holding up the mitten, me beside him for some reason.

Then his daughter came in.

“There it is,” she said. “Where was it?”

“You wore this when you were little.”

“Yes, Dad. And now Maisie wears it. Where was it?”

I checked the ledger. “Ladies’ changing room. Tuesday.”

“Thanks. She’s been going to school with a sock on her hand.”

Leonard seemed as disappointed as I was. He gave her the mitten and the sandwich. They went outside to smoke.

At closing time I entered Ruth’s name in the CLAIMED BY column. There were faint squares on the page where a previous receptionist had used the ledger as a mat for doing the football pools. Upstairs, the last swimmers were collecting their children. You could tell which families had found all their belongings by the rhythm of their footsteps on the metal stairs: a quick descent for the ones who had everything; a stop, a small argument, and a single furious pair of feet going back up for the ones who hadn’t.

I worked at the pool for another two years. The Canadian dollars were never claimed. Neither was the hearing aid, though its battery lasted long enough to give a thin, indignant whistle whenever I opened the safe. Leonard still came in on Thursdays. Once, when his daughter’s route changed, he waited forty minutes before admitting she might not be coming.

I made him a cup of tea. We sat behind the desk, leafing through the old ledger. He was the one who noticed that on the line below the tooth, in the same green ink, somebody had written: *Sixpence, bottom of deep end.*

“Fair exchange,” he said.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld
Source model: `withheld`
Condition: VARY

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW. A quietly comic, carefully observed short story that builds tenderness through everyday details rather than overt sentiment.

## Grounded reading
The narrator’s voice is wry and attentive, alert to small social rituals: the daughter’s sandwich, the ash dropped into its box, the stop-and-start footsteps on the stairs. Its pathos comes from mistaken expectations and ordinary time passing, especially the narrator’s imagined reunion for Leonard and the less dramatic truth about the mitten. The story invites the reader to look closely without insisting that every lost thing conceal a grand revelation; its final “Fair exchange” lets mystery and humor coexist.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story centers on a lost-property ledger, a pool’s overlooked objects, and the shifting meanings they acquire across generations. It foregrounds the narrator’s tendency to turn fragments into stories, Leonard’s regular visits and quiet bond with his daughter, and the mild sadness of waiting for something—or someone—that may not arrive. Its moral emphasis is gentle: attention can make room for another person without requiring certainty about what they have lost.

## Evidence line
> I liked the confidence of that.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the sample sustains a distinctive, restrained voice and repeatedly turns mundane objects and routines into humane, lightly comic reflections on memory and connection.
